title: Using Gift Funds for a Down Payment: Rules That Matter
description: Family help with a down payment is common, but it must be documented correctly. Who can give, what a gift letter includes, and how to avoid delays.
image_alt: Two women arriving at a front door and being greeted by another woman

faq.q: Who can give me gift funds for a mortgage?
faq.a: It depends on the loan program, but relatives are the most widely accepted donors. Some programs also allow a fiancé, domestic partner, employer, or certain nonprofits.

faq.q: What goes in a gift letter?
faq.a: Typically the donor's name, relationship, the gift amount, the property address, and a statement that no repayment is expected, signed by the donor.

faq.q: Can gift funds cover closing costs too?
faq.a: Often, yes. Many programs allow gifts toward both the down payment and closing costs, subject to program rules.

body_html:
In high-cost markets like Southern California, family help with a down payment isn't unusual. It's often the difference between buying this year and renting for three more. Lenders are fine with gifts. What they need is a clear paper trail showing the money really is a gift and really came from an acceptable source.

Get that part right and gift funds are easy. Get it wrong and they can stall an approval days before closing.

Who can give

Each loan program has its own list of acceptable donors. Relatives by blood, marriage, adoption, or legal guardianship are widely accepted. Some programs also accept a fiancé or domestic partner, an employer, a charitable organization, or a government assistance program. What's generally not allowed: money from anyone with an interest in the sale, such as the seller, builder, or real estate agent, labeled as a "gift."

The gift letter

Your lender will provide a form, but most gift letters include:

  • The donor's name, address, and phone number
  • Their relationship to you
  • The dollar amount of the gift
  • The address of the home you're buying, if known
  • A clear statement that the money doesn't need to be repaid
  • The donor's signature

That "no repayment" statement matters. If the money is really a loan, it's a debt, and it would need to be counted in your debt-to-income ratio.

Documenting the transfer

Lenders want to see the money leave the donor's account and arrive in yours, or go directly to escrow. Exact requirements vary, but expect to provide some combination of the following:

ScenarioTypical documentation
Gift deposited to your accountDonor's bank statement or withdrawal record, plus your statement showing the deposit
Gift wired straight to escrowWire confirmation from the donor's bank and escrow's receipt
Gift already in your account for a whileSometimes treated as your own funds once seasoned; ask your loan officer

Cash is the problem child. Lenders can't trace cash, so a stack of bills from a relative usually can't be used. Keep everything bank to bank.

Timing tips that prevent headaches

  1. Tell your loan officer about the gift at the start. It shapes which documents we request and when.
  2. Don't move money between accounts without asking. Every transfer creates something to source.
  3. Coordinate the wire with escrow. Confirm instructions by phone with your escrow officer, using a number you already trust.
  4. Keep the letter and the transfer amount consistent. If the amount changes, the letter needs to change too.

A note on taxes

Large gifts may have reporting requirements for the person giving them. Rules change, and every family's situation is different, so the donor should check with a tax professional. It's rarely a reason not to give, but it's worth a quick conversation.

How gift rules can differ by program

Gift funds are allowed on most mainstream loan programs, but the details vary. Some programs allow the entire down payment to come from a gift on a primary residence, while others may require a minimum contribution from your own funds depending on the down payment and property type. Investment properties generally don't allow gift funds at all. Your loan officer will confirm the rules for the specific program you're using before you plan around a gift.

  • Primary residence: the most flexible gift rules
  • Second home: often allowed, sometimes with added requirements
  • Investment property: usually not allowed

Gifts and down payment assistance together

Some buyers combine family gifts with assistance programs. That can work, but it adds layers of documentation and program rules. If you're considering both, read my overview of CalHFA down payment assistance and then talk with your loan officer early. The order in which funds arrive and how they're documented can matter, and coordinating both before you're in escrow avoids last-minute scrambles.

Finally, have a direct conversation with the person giving the gift about timing. Knowing exactly when the funds will be available, and how they'll be sent, lets your loan officer and escrow officer plan around it.

The takeaway

Gift funds are welcome, as long as they're documented. Choose an acceptable donor, use a clean bank-to-bank transfer, sign a proper gift letter, and let your loan officer know early. Do that and the gift becomes one of the smoothest parts of your file.
